# SkillEvaluator ![SkillEvaluator wordmark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator/ad2815fe78c045db91d230681d32863698da08cf/docs/assets/skillevaluator-wordmark.svg) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-Apache%202.0-green.svg)](LICENSE) [![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-3.12%20%7C%203.13%20%7C%203.14-blue.svg)](https://www.python.org/) [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/skillevaluator.svg?label=PyPI)](https://pypi.org/project/skillevaluator/) [![Documentation](https://img.shields.io/badge/Documentation-docs.nvidia.com-blue.svg)](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/) [![Paper](https://img.shields.io/badge/arXiv-2608.20614-b31b1b.svg)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20614) [![NVIDIA Developer Blog](https://img.shields.io/badge/Blog-NVIDIA%20Developer-76B900.svg)](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/evaluating-ai-agent-skill-performance-with-nvidia-skillevaluator/) > 📺 **Livestream:** [Ask the Experts: Evaluating Agent Skills](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4rI0zATFxYI) SkillEvaluator checks AI agent skills and measures their effect on task results: start with quality checks, then compare runs with and without a skill. Agent skills are folders of instructions and supporting files defined by the [Agent Skills specification](https://agentskills.io/). SkillEvaluator is part of the [NVIDIA Verified Skills pipeline](https://github.com/NVIDIA/skills). ## Get started Three ways in, one CLI, same results.
1. Run the CLI directly 2. Add it to your repo via CI 3. Wire it to your agent
Install (or `uv tool install`): ```bash pip install skillevaluator ``` Run all Tier 1 checks, no API key: ```bash skillevaluator validate \ ./my-skill --tiers 1 ``` Or run from a clone: [Quickstart](#quickstart). Check changed skills on every pull request. On GitHub, run: ```bash skillevaluator ci init ``` It opens a setup PR. On GitLab, copy the [CI template](https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator/tree/main/ci/bundles/0.9.0). Add the [SkillEvaluator skill](skills/skillevaluator/) to Claude Code, Codex or any skill-aware agent: ```bash npx skills add \ NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator ``` Then ask: *"Is my skill any good?"* No Node.js? [Copy the folder](docs/agent-skill.mdx#install).
Guides: [installation](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/installation), [CI setup](docs/cli-onboarding.mdx) ([GitHub](docs/github-actions.mdx), [GitLab](docs/gitlab-ci.mdx), [report examples](ci/examples/README.md)) and [agent skill](docs/agent-skill.mdx). ## Quickstart Both paths use bundled `text-analyzer`. | Start here | Requires | First result | | --- | --- | --- | | [Run without an LLM](#run-without-an-llm) | Git and uv | A deterministic quality score and findings | | [Use NVIDIA Build](#use-nvidia-build) | Git, uv, and a Build API key | Model-backed rubric scores and feedback | Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) and Git, then get the example: ```bash git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator.git cd SkillEvaluator ``` uv provisions Python 3.13 and dependencies. For standalone installation, see [Installation](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/installation). ### Run without an LLM ```bash uv run --python 3.13 skillevaluator quality-check \ src/skillevaluator/tier3/reference_skills/text-analyzer \ -r cli -r json -o reports/first-quality ``` No API key, scanner, GPU or Docker is needed. The example scores **86.2/100 (B)**, exits `0` and saves `reports/first-quality/skillevaluator-quality.json`. The passing threshold defaults to 70. This checks static quality; publication evidence stays `INCOMPLETE`. Security needs scanners; agent impact needs live evaluation. Replace the example path with your skill directory. See the [keyless walkthrough](docs/quickstart.mdx#run-without-an-llm). ### Use NVIDIA Build Eligible NVIDIA Developer Program members can use NVIDIA-hosted endpoints for **free prototyping**, subject to [access terms and rate limits](https://docs.api.nvidia.com/nim/docs/product). 1. Sign in at [build.nvidia.com](https://build.nvidia.com/) and complete enrollment. 2. Open a model page, select **Get API Key**, and generate your key. 3. Set the provider and key in the same terminal, then run the rubric check: ```bash export SKILL_EVAL_LLM_PROVIDER=nv_build export NVIDIA_API_KEY='nvapi-...' uv run --python 3.13 --extra llm skillevaluator rubric-eval \ src/skillevaluator/tier3/reference_skills/text-analyzer \ -r cli -r json -o reports/first-build ``` The command sends skill documentation to the model and saves feedback in `reports/first-build/skillevaluator-rubric.json`. No agent runtime or Docker is needed. Completed evaluations can still fail rubric thresholds. The same key supports Tier 2 embeddings and supported Tier 3 agents. See the [Build walkthrough](docs/quickstart.mdx#use-nvidia-build) or [provider configuration](docs/configuration.mdx). ## Three-tier overview ![SkillEvaluator three-tier pipeline: Skill → Tier 1 Validation → Tier 2 Deduplication → Tier 3 Live Evaluation → Reports](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator/ad2815fe78c045db91d230681d32863698da08cf/docs/assets/three-tier-overview.svg) Each tier is independent. Add its extra to your command: | Tier | Question | Example after setup | Additional setup | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Tier 1: Validation | Is the skill safe, well-formed and [harness-compatible](docs/tier1-validation.mdx#the-checks)? | `uv run skillevaluator tier1 ./my-skill --no-llm` | External scanners for full static coverage; a provider and model clients enable LLM checks | | Tier 2: Deduplication | Does guidance repeat or overlap? | `uv run --extra tier2 skillevaluator tier2 ./my-skill` | Embeddings and chat; add `--catalog ./skill-catalog.json` for inter-skill comparison | | Tier 3: Live Evaluation | Does the skill help the agent? | `uv run --extra tier3 skillevaluator tier3 ./my-skill` | Provider access, a supported agent, and a running sandbox (Docker by default) | Tier 1 fetches pinned, verified SkillSpector and Gitleaks releases when they are missing; Semgrep is optional. See [scanners](docs/installation.mdx#system-tools). `--no-llm` does not remove scanner requirements; a scanner that cannot run is `INCOMPLETE` and exits nonzero. [SkillSpector](https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillSpector) provides specialized skill security scanning; [Harbor](https://github.com/harbor-framework/harbor), the open-source agent evaluation framework, powers sandboxed agent runs. Tier 2 reports when inter-skill comparison did not run. Tier 3 autopilot reuses sources or creates one skill-grounded case with limited coverage. See [tier guides](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/). ## Run the combined pipeline After setting up the provider, scanners, and agent sandbox, run all three tiers: ```bash uv run --python 3.13 --extra all skillevaluator doctor --env-mode docker uv run --python 3.13 --extra all skillevaluator validate ./my-skill ``` `doctor` checks readiness, not inference success. `validate` runs all tiers with autopilot for skills. Use `--tiers 1,2` to skip live evaluation or `--tiers 1` for static checks. `--no-autopilot` requires an existing source. Other artifact types retain their applicable stages. Tier 1 gates `validate`. Tier 2 gates unless `--no-block-on-dedup` is set; Tier 3 gates only with `--block-on-agent-eval`. Model and managed-sandbox usage can incur charges; see [runtime and cost](docs/tier3-live-evaluation.mdx#plan-for-cost). Standalone generation needs substantive `evals/EVAL.md` guidance, a `--prompt` file with task requests and outcomes, or matching retained traces. `--force` below replaces the autopilot starter; `--refine` refines it. Explicit `--grounding skill` permits skill-only starters. Review cases; templates omit unauthored negatives. ```bash uv run --python 3.13 --extra tier3 skillevaluator tier3 create-eval-dataset ./my-skill --full --prompt eval-guidance.md --force ``` ## Run from a source checkout Use `uv run --python 3.13` with the relevant extra. See [Installation](docs/installation.mdx#choosing-extras) for extras and standalone upgrades. ## Research and citation Resources: [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.20614), [PDF](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.20614), [DOI](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2608.20614), [BibTeX](https://arxiv.org/bibtex/2608.20614), and the [NVIDIA Developer blog](https://developer.nvidia.com/blog/evaluating-ai-agent-skill-performance-with-nvidia-skillevaluator/). Cite the paper and record the SkillEvaluator release or commit; see [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff). ## Documentation See [the documentation](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/) for setup, tier guides, reports, CI integration, CLI reference, and [performance dashboard](docs/reports.mdx#performance-dashboard). ## Installation and third-party software Follow the [installation guide](https://docs.nvidia.com/skills/skillevaluator/installation) to choose the full installation or a smaller per-tier setup. This project will download and install additional third-party open source software projects. Review the license terms of these open source projects before use. ## Contributing Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) and run: ```bash make lint && make test && make build ``` See [project governance](GOVERNANCE.md) and the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). ## Support Support level: **Experimental**. Community-supported, best-effort, with no SLA or NVIDIA enterprise support entitlement. Report bugs and feature requests through [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator/issues); see [SUPPORT.md](SUPPORT.md). ## Security Report suspected vulnerabilities using the private process in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md). Do not disclose security issues in a public GitHub issue. ## Releases Release changes are recorded in [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md) and [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/NVIDIA/SkillEvaluator/releases). ## License Apache License 2.0 — see [LICENSE](LICENSE), [NOTICE](NOTICE), and [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). # Stitch Design Skills A collection of agent skills and plugins for [Google Stitch](https://stitch.withgoogle.com), following the [Agent Skills](https://agentskills.io) open standard. Compatible with coding agents such as Codex, Antigravity, Gemini CLI, Claude Code, Cursor, and OpenCode (manual install). ## Quick Start ### 1. Install Plugins (Recommended) The fastest way to set up the full Stitch plugin suite globally. #### Codex Add the Stitch Skills marketplace, then install the plugins you need.
Via CLI (recommended) ```bash codex plugin marketplace add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --ref main \ --sparse .agents/plugins \ --sparse plugins/stitch-design \ --sparse plugins/stitch-build \ --sparse plugins/stitch-utilities ``` > [!TIP] > The `--sparse` flags are optional — they limit the checkout to only the > listed paths for a faster clone. Omit them to pull the entire repository.
Via the Codex UI Navigate to **Settings → Plugin Marketplaces → Add** and fill in: | Field | Value | |---|---| | **Source** | `https://github.com/google-labs-code/stitch-skills` | | **Git ref** | `main` | | **Sparse paths** | *(optional)* `.agents/plugins`, `plugins/stitch-design`, `plugins/stitch-build`, `plugins/stitch-utilities` |
Once the marketplace is registered, install any combination of: - **`stitch-design`** — design-focused skills - **`stitch-build`** — build and component skills - **`stitch-utilities`** — utility and helper skills #### Claude Code & Cursor ```bash # Claude Code — installs into the current project npx plugins add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --scope project --target claude-code ``` ```bash # Cursor — installs into the current workspace npx plugins add google-labs-code/stitch-skills --scope workspace --target cursor ``` #### OpenCode OpenCode does **not** use `npx plugins` / `npx skills` or the Codex/Claude marketplace layout. Install skills and the Stitch MCP server manually: **1. Skills** — copy the skill folders you need into a discoverable path: ```bash # Project-local (recommended) mkdir -p .opencode/skills cp -R plugins/stitch-design/skills/generate-design .opencode/skills/generate-design # repeat for other skills under plugins/*/skills/ ``` OpenCode also discovers `.claude/skills/` and `.agents/skills/` (see [OpenCode skills docs](https://opencode.ai/docs/skills/)). > **Naming:** OpenCode requires skill `name` frontmatter to be lowercase kebab-case and match the directory name. Skills that use `stitch::…` names (or other non-kebab forms) need the `name` field and folder renamed before OpenCode will load them. Extra frontmatter such as `allowed-tools` is ignored. **2. Stitch MCP** — add a remote MCP entry in project `opencode.json` or `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` after completing the [Stitch MCP setup](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/mcp/setup/): ```json { "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json", "mcp": { "stitch": { "type": "remote", "url": "YOUR_STITCH_MCP_URL", "enabled": true } } } ``` Replace `YOUR_STITCH_MCP_URL` with the endpoint from the Stitch MCP setup flow (credentials/env vars from that guide still apply). Tool names inside skill instructions may differ from OpenCode builtins (`webfetch` / `bash` instead of `web_fetch` / `run_command`). Prefer the OpenCode tool names when adapting a skill for OpenCode. ### 2. Install Skills Selectively Choose only the specific skills you need. > [!IMPORTANT] > Stitch Design Skills often have inter-dependencies. If you choose to install skills selectively, ensure you include all required dependencies. ```bash npx skills add google-labs-code/stitch-skills ``` You can run the following commands to see the help documentation for plugins and skills: ```bash npx plugins --help npx skills --help ``` ## Prerequisites These skills require the **Stitch MCP** server to be configured and running in your agent's environment. Make sure you have followed the [Stitch MCP Setup Instructions](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/mcp/setup/) to register the server and set up appropriate environment variables and credentials. > **Docs navigation:** If a link on [stitch.withgoogle.com/docs](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/) redirects incorrectly, open the target path under the same host (e.g. `https://stitch.withgoogle.com/docs/learn/device-types/`). ## Available Plugins ### Design (`stitch-design`) Core design workflows for creating, managing, and optimizing designs within Stitch. | Skill | Description | Prompt Example | |---|---|---| | [stitch::code-to-design](plugins/stitch-design/skills/code-to-design/) | Convert frontend code (React, Vue, etc.) to a Stitch Design via HTML extraction + design system + upload | *"Upload the frontend code at `/path/to/dashboard` into a Stitch project named 'Dashboard-Migration-2026'."* | | [stitch::generate-design](plugins/stitch-design/skills/generate-design/) | Generate new screens from text or images, edit existing screens, and create design variants | · *"Make a browse tab for a mobile app for romance and date night ideas."*
· *"Edit the login screen to add a 'Remember Me' checkbox and change the button color to blue."*
· *"Generate 3 design variants of the home screen with dark mode and high-density layouts."* | | [stitch::manage-design-system](plugins/stitch-design/skills/manage-design-system/) | Manage design systems in Stitch — upload DESIGN.md and apply themes to screens | *"Upload our design system from `.stitch/DESIGN.md` and apply it to all screens."* | | [stitch::extract-design-md](plugins/stitch-design/skills/extract-design-md/) | Extract a comprehensive DESIGN.md directly from frontend source code | *"Scan `/src` and extract the design system into `.stitch/DESIGN.md`."* | | [stitch::extract-static-html](plugins/stitch-design/skills/extract-static-html/) | Extract self-contained static HTML from running web apps, inlining CSS and images | *"Extract a static HTML snapshot of `http://localhost:3000/profile`."* | | [stitch::upload-to-stitch](plugins/stitch-design/skills/upload-to-stitch/) | Upload local assets (images, mockups, HTML) to a Stitch project | *"Upload `.stitch/landing_page.html` to Stitch project `projects/987654321`."* | --- ### Build (`stitch-build`) Code generation, framework integration, and asset compilation from Stitch designs. | Skill | Description | Prompt Example | |---|---|---| | [stitch::react-components](plugins/stitch-build/skills/react-components/) | Convert Stitch screens to React component systems with automated validation and design token consistency | · *"Convert all screens in Stitch project `projects/123` to React components."*
· *"Sync the app to the last updates of the Stitch project `13039335308618232534`."* | | [stitch::react-native](plugins/stitch-build/skills/react-native/) | Convert Stitch HTML designs to production-ready React Native components with StyleSheet and platform-specific code | · *"Convert the Stitch design to React Native components with proper theme and navigation."*
· *"Sync the app to the last updates of the Stitch project `13039335308618232534`."* | | [remotion](plugins/stitch-build/skills/remotion/) | Generate walkthrough videos from Stitch projects using Remotion with smooth transitions and zooming | *"Generate a walkthrough video of the Stitch project `projects/456`."* | | [shadcn-ui](plugins/stitch-build/skills/shadcn-ui/) | Expert guidance for integrating and building applications with shadcn/ui components | *"Set up shadcn/ui and build a data table with sorting and filtering."* | | [react-vite-dashboard](plugins/stitch-build/skills/react-vite-dashboard/) | Convert Stitch screens to React + Vite dashboards with TanStack Query, DESIGN.md tokens, and Web3 read patterns | *"Build a DeFi portfolio dashboard from this Stitch screen using our DESIGN.md."* | --- ### Utilities (`stitch-utilities`) Supporting tools for enhancing prompts, generating design specs, and enforcing design standards. | Skill | Description | Prompt Example | |---|---|---| | [design-md](plugins/stitch-utilities/skills/design-md/) | Analyze Stitch projects and generate comprehensive DESIGN.md files in semantic language | *"Analyze Stitch project `projects/123` and generate a DESIGN.md."* | | [enhance-prompt](plugins/stitch-utilities/skills/enhance-prompt/) | Transform vague UI ideas into polished, Stitch-optimized prompts with UI/UX keywords | *"Enhance this prompt: 'make a settings page'."* | | [stitch-loop](plugins/stitch-utilities/skills/stitch-loop/) | Generate complete multi-page websites from a single prompt with automated validation | *"Build a 5-page portfolio website with Stitch."* | | [taste-design](plugins/stitch-utilities/skills/taste-design/) | Generate DESIGN.md files enforcing premium, anti-generic UI standards | *"Generate a premium DESIGN.md with strict typography and calibrated colors."* | ## Repository Structure ```text plugins/ ├── stitch-design/ — Core design workflow plugin │ ├── plugin.json │ └── skills/ │ ├── code-to-design/ │ ├── generate-design/ │ ├── manage-design-system/ │ ├── extract-design-md/ │ ├── extract-static-html/ │ └── upload-to-stitch/ ├── stitch-build/ — Code generation & build plugin │ ├── plugin.json │ └── skills/ │ ├── react-components/ — stitch::react-components │ ├── react-native/ │ ├── react-vite-dashboard/ │ ├── remotion/ │ └── shadcn-ui/ └── stitch-utilities/ — Design utilities & assistants plugin ├── plugin.json └── skills/ ├── design-md/ ├── enhance-prompt/ ├── stitch-loop/ └── taste-design/ ``` Each skill follows the Agent Skills standard: ```text skills// ├── SKILL.md — The "Mission Control" for the agent ├── scripts/ — Executable enforcers (Validation & Networking) ├── resources/ — The knowledge base (Checklists & Style Guides) └── examples/ — The "Gold Standard" syntactically valid references ``` ## Adding New Skills All new skills need to follow the file structure above to implement the Agent Skills open standard. ### Great candidates for new skills * **Validation**: Skills that convert Stitch HTML to other UI frameworks and validate the syntax. * **Decoupling Data**: Skills that convert static design content into external mock data files. * **Generate Designs**: Skills that generate new design screens in Stitch from a given set of data. This is not an officially supported Google product. This project is not eligible for the [Google Open Source Software Vulnerability Rewards Program](https://bughunters.google.com/open-source-security).

# AG-UI: The Agent-User Interaction Protocol AG-UI is an open, lightweight, event-based protocol that standardizes how AI agents connect to user-facing applications. Built for simplicity and flexibility, it enables seamless integration between AI agents, real time user context, and user interfaces. ---

[![Version](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@ag-ui/core?label=Version&color=6963ff&logo=npm&logoColor=white)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@ag-ui/core) ![MIT](https://img.shields.io/github/license/copilotkit/copilotkit?color=%236963ff&label=License) ![Discord](https://img.shields.io/discord/1379082175625953370?logo=discord&logoColor=%23FFFFFF&label=Discord&color=%236963ff) Join our Discord →     Read the Docs →     Go to the AG-UI Dojo →     Follow us → ## 🚀 Getting Started Create a new AG-UI application in seconds: ```bash npx create-ag-ui-app my-agent-app ```

Useful Links:

- [The AG-UI Dojo](https://dojo.ag-ui.com/) - [Build AG-UI-powered applications(Quickstart)](https://docs.ag-ui.com/quickstart/applications) - [Build new AG-UI framework integrations (Quickstart)](https://go.copilotkit.ai/agui-contribute) - [Book a call to discuss an AG-UI integration with a new framework](https://calendly.com/markus-copilotkit/ag-ui) - [Join the Discord Community](https://discord.gg/Jd3FzfdJa8) ## What is AG-UI? AG-UI is an open, lightweight, event-based protocol for agent-human interaction, designed for simplicity & flexibility: - During agent executions, agent backends **emit events _compatible_ with one of AG-UI's ~16 standard event types** - Agent backends can **accept one of a few simple AG-UI compatible inputs** as arguments **AG-UI includes a flexible middleware layer** that ensures compatibility across diverse environments: - Works with **any event transport** (SSE, WebSockets, webhooks, etc.) - Allows for **loose event format matching**, enabling broad agent and app interoperability It also ships with a **reference HTTP implementation** and **default connector** to help teams get started fast. [Learn more about the specs →](https://go.copilotkit.ai/ag-ui-introduction) ## Why AG-UI? AG-UI was developed based on real-world requirements and practical experience building in-app agent interactions. ## Where does AGUI fit in the agentic protocol stack? AG-UI is complementary to the other 2 top agentic protocols - MCP gives agents tools - A2A allows agents to communicate with other agents - AG-UI brings agents into user-facing applications
## 🚀 Features - 💬 Real-time agentic chat with streaming - 🔄 Bi-directional state synchronization - 🧩 Generative UI and structured messages - 🧠 Real-time context enrichment - 🛠️ Frontend tool integration - 🧑‍💻 Human-in-the-loop collaboration ## 🛠 Supported Integrations AG-UI was born from CopilotKit's initial **partnership** with LangChain and CrewAI - and brings the incredibly popular agent-user-interactivity infrastructure to the wider agentic ecosystem. **1st party** = the platforms that have AG‑UI built in and provide documentation for guidance. ## Frameworks | Framework | Studio | Quickstart | Showcase | Playground | Catalog | Docs | Discord

Download the desktop app: macOS · Windows · Linux (.deb)

HyperFrames is a free, open-source framework for turning HTML, CSS, media, and seekable animations into deterministic MP4 videos. Use it locally with the CLI, from AI coding agents with skills, or as the rendering core behind hosted authoring workflows. The [HyperFrames Studio app](https://hyperframes.heygen.com/studio-app) is free to use as well; its [Pro plan](https://hyperframes.studio/pricing) adds HeyGen's top video, image, voice and music models. Using Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or another coding agent? Run `npx hyperframes skills update` once, then ask your agent to make a video. ## Quick Start ### With an AI coding agent For Claude Code, install the versioned plugin: ```bash claude plugin marketplace add heygen-com/hyperframes claude plugin install hyperframes@hyperframes ``` To enable auto-update for the **hyperframes** marketplace, run `claude` in a terminal in your project. In Claude Code's terminal UI, run `/plugin`, then select **Marketplaces** → **hyperframes** → **Enable auto-update**. Afterward, use `/hyperframes:hyperframes`. See the [plugin guide](docs/guides/plugins.mdx) for Copilot, VS Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, updates, and migration. For standalone skills (including OpenCode), use: ```bash npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes ``` > The picker opens with nothing pre-selected — the **Core Skills** group is all you need; `/slideshow`, `/remotion-to-hyperframes` and `/figma` install on demand. Without the picker (a script or a CI job), `npx hyperframes skills update` installs exactly the core set, whereas `skills add --all` installs all 9 published skills. The six repo-internal skills under `.claude/skills` / `.agents/skills` are excluded by default. For the full published set use `npx hyperframes skills`. > > `skills add` resolves the skills.sh registry blob, which can lag `main` by hours. `npx hyperframes skills update` installs the skills from the release tag that matches your CLI version, so they match the CLI that runs them. Run project-local installs from your video project's directory. From a HyperFrames checkout, use `npx hyperframes skills update` for a global install instead: a project-local installer target can overlap the tracked `skills/` source and overwrite uncommitted edits. See [contributor setup](CONTRIBUTING.md#getting-started). Try a prompt like: > Using `/hyperframes`, create a 10-second product intro with a fade-in title, a background video, and subtle background music. The skills teach agents the HyperFrames production loop: plan the video, write valid HTML, wire seekable animations, add media, lint, preview, and render. They work with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, IBM Bob, and other coding agents that support skills. ## Skills HyperFrames ships 9 skills. Make any video by asking for it; the `/hyperframes` skill carries the contract and the references (film, captions, overlays, motion, look). Read it first. For standalone installation, default to the **core set** (`/hyperframes`, `/hyperframes-cli`, `/hyperframes-registry`, `/media-use`, `/reverse-any-video`, `/style-sampling`). `npx hyperframes skills update` installs exactly that from anywhere; the interactive picker (`npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes`) lists it as the "Core Skills" group, nothing pre-selected. The picker is interactive-only — a non-interactive or agent run without `--skill` installs all 9. Use `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --all` to install the complete published set deliberately (skips the picker), or `npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes --skill ` for just one (bare name, no leading `/`). Standalone installs stay lean after that: `npx hyperframes init` installs the **core set** only when it is missing and never touches a skill you already have (`npx hyperframes skills update` refreshes them, and never removes one); `/figma`, `/slideshow` and `/remotion-to-hyperframes` install **on demand** with `npx hyperframes skills update `. Nothing re-pulls the full set behind your back. ### Plugin packages Plugins bundle the full skill catalog and use their agent's update manager. `bun run package:agent-plugin` builds the committed portable ZIP, source metadata, and SHA-256 checksum. See the [maintainer checklist](docs/contributing/agent-plugins.mdx). ### Upload to Codex Build the upload-ready Codex plugin archive from the committed `HEAD` version of the manifest, brand assets, and skills: ```bash bun run package:codex-plugin ``` This writes `dist/hyperframes-plugin.zip` with a `hyperframes/` root folder and fails if the archive exceeds Codex's 100 MB upload limit. ### Core set | Skill | Use when | | ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `/hyperframes` | **Read first** for any request to make, edit, animate or render a video, motion graphic, captions or overlays with HyperFrames (HTML rendered to video). Holds the render contract and the work loop, and points to the references for format, motion, look, captions, whole films and storyboards. | | `/hyperframes-cli` | The HyperFrames CLI by job — scaffold, check, look at frames, edit the timeline, preview, render locally or in the cloud, share, project history — plus reading its JSON and recovering from build or render failures. | | `/hyperframes-registry` | About 450 ready-made blocks and components installed as editable source — transitions, overlays, titles, kinetic type, captions, charts, maps, 3D, camera moves. Use before hand-building any named visual; also for `hyperframes add` and `catalog`. | | `/media-use` | Get or make any media for a video — music, sound effects, images, icons, logos, voiceover, avatar and generated video, transcripts, cutouts, colour grades and looks — with HeyGen or free local tools, and mix placed audio. Also for footage that looks dark, flat or dull. | | `/reverse-any-video` | Rebuilding any video file as an editable HyperFrames project (motion graphics, talking heads, live action, AI-generated footage), checked frame by frame against the original. HyperFrames Pro. | | `/style-sampling` | Making a new episode on your topic in one of five proven styles: Collage Explainer, Finance Explainer, Animated Science Explainer, 3D Brand Explainer, 3D True Crime. HyperFrames Pro. | ### On demand | Skill | Use when | | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `/figma` | Bring Figma into a video — rendered assets, brand tokens, components, storyboard frames as reconstructed motion, shaders and connector-assisted motion. Use when you paste a figma.com link. | | `/slideshow` | A presentation, pitch deck or interactive deck — discrete slides, fragment reveals, branching, hotspot navigation, presenter mode with speaker notes. repository.description: Hardware ray-traced three.js: a real-time path tracer behind a three.js-style API. Rust + wgpu engine, TypeScript scene and gameplay packages.

details.readme:
ThreeRT

Hardware ray-traced three.js.

A real-time path tracer behind a three.js-style API. Write the scene you would write in three.js,
and every light in it is traced on the GPU's ray-tracing hardware, at 60 fps.

Website · Apps · Download · Docs · Discord · X


ThreeRT, live on an Apple M3 Max: this repository's demos and OpenStrike, a shooter built on the engine.

## Three + RT **Three**, for the API you already know. **RT**, for the three things it adds: - **Ray tracing.** Every light is traced: shadows, bounce light, reflections, and glowing surfaces that light the room. No shadow maps, no light probes, no lightmaps, no baking. - **Real time.** 60 fps in production scenes with the camera moving: Amazon Lumberyard Bistro and Beeple's Zero-Day, on a laptop. Not a still that converges once you stop. - **Runtime.** A game runtime, not only a renderer. Scene code and game logic run inside the engine, and the same file runs as plain three.js in any browser. ## Hello world looks right Write a scene at tutorial size and leave every setting at its default. ```ts import { Scene, PerspectiveCamera, Mesh, BoxGeometry, MeshStandardMaterial, DirectionalLight, SkyAtmosphere } from "@threert/scene"; export default function build() { const scene = new Scene(); const sun = new DirectionalLight(0xffffff, 90000).setSunAngles(28, 100); // lux scene.add(sun); scene.environment = new SkyAtmosphere({ sun }); const plaster = new MeshStandardMaterial({ color: 0xd9d4cc, roughness: 0.92 }); const wall = new Mesh(new BoxGeometry(6.6, 3, 0.3), plaster); wall.position.set(0, 1.5, -3.15); scene.add(wall); // ... the rest of the room: a floor, a window, a sofa, a lamp const camera = new PerspectiveCamera(58, 16 / 9, 0.05, 200); camera.position.set(-2.3, 1.45, 2.4); camera.lookAt(1.0, 0.9, -1.2); scene.add(camera); return { scene, camera }; } ``` | three.js, as written | ThreeRT, all defaults | |---|---| | ![A room in three.js: flat walls, no sunlight on the floor](site/media/hello/sun-room-three.webp) | ![The same room in ThreeRT: sunlight through the window, bounce light on the walls](site/media/hello/sun-room-rt.webp) | The sun through the window, the sky, the bounce light off the floor and the lamp's glow come from tracing the scene. Light is in physical units: the sun is 90,000 lux, and an emissive surface is a light source. The whole file is [`scenes/sun-room.ts`](scenes/sun-room.ts). ## Against three.js at full power The same scene file, run by both engines on the same Mac. three.js gets everything it has: shadow maps, image-based lighting and, on WebGPU, its own SSGI, SSR and TRAA. | three.js r187 | ThreeRT | |---|---| | ![Amazon Lumberyard Bistro at night in three.js](site/media/bistro/hero-three.webp) | ![The same frame in ThreeRT](site/media/bistro/hero-rt.webp) | | ![Beeple's Zero-Day in three.js](site/media/zero-day/tuned.webp) | ![The same frame in ThreeRT](site/media/zero-day/live.webp) | | Bistro night, 1280 × 720 | Frame cost | Error against the reference (ΔE, lower is closer) | |---|---|---:| | **ThreeRT, live** | 15.5 ms (60 fps) | **3.4** | | three.js, WebGPU + SSGI + SSR + TRAA | 34.7 ms (29 fps) | 10.1 | | three.js, WebGL tuned | 15.9 ms (60 fps) | 12.1 | The reference is an unbiased offline render (4,096 samples per pixel, no denoiser). The method, every scene, and where three.js is ahead (it draws small scenes in about 1 ms) are in [`docs/COMPARE.md`](docs/COMPARE.md). ## Get started ### Play and make games 1. **[Download ThreeRT](https://threert.dev/download/)** for macOS (14 or later, Apple silicon) or iPhone and iPad (iOS 17 or later). The client fetches a game's code and traces it on the device's own GPU. 2. Open an example from the app's library or from [threert.app](https://threert.app), where ThreeRT apps and games are published. 3. Write your own with the `threert` command line that ships inside the Mac app: ```bash threert create my-game cd my-game threert dev # bundles on save, serves every client on your network, prints a QR code for your phone ``` The same address in any browser shows the game as three.js. The full walk-through is at [threert.dev/docs](https://threert.dev/docs/). ### Packages | Package | What | |---|---| | [`@threert/scene`](packages/scene) | The three.js-style scene API: meshes, PBR materials, lights, glTF models, physics, volumes | | [`@threert/gameplay`](packages/gameplay) | Games: state, transactional handlers, world handlers, frame scripts; input, a HUD and a channel to the app that runs the game; deterministic and replayable | | [`@threert/voxel`](packages/voxel) | Destructible voxel levels: explosions, cuts, and pieces that break off as rigid bodies | ```bash npm install @threert/scene @threert/gameplay ``` `threert dev` bundles these for you. Install them from npm for types, tests, or a build pipeline of your own. ### Build the engine from source The engine is Rust and [wgpu](https://wgpu.rs): hardware ray queries where the GPU has them (Metal, Vulkan), a software BVH where it does not. You need Rust, Node 24 and [Bun](https://bun.sh). ```bash npm install && bun scripts/setup.ts # assets/ -> the machine's shared asset store, then fetch what is missing node tools/build-scenes.ts # scenes/*.ts + games -> out/bundles/.js bun renderer/build.ts # -> renderer/target/release/threert-render renderer/target/release/threert-render play out/bundles/light-room.js # a game, in a window renderer/target/release/threert-render render out/bundles/cornell-box.js -o out/cornell.png --spp 32 # a scene, to an image node tools/three/open.ts scenes/bistro.ts # the same scene in three.js, in your browser ``` In the window: drag to orbit, right-drag to pan, wheel to zoom, WASD/QE to fly, `R` to reset, `P` for a snapshot. ```bash npm test && npm run typecheck && (cd renderer && cargo test --release) # scene API, gameplay, runtime and engine tests npm run test:render # the render test suite, on the GPU ``` ## # OpenVideoHarness ### Making one good film is easy. Making a good one every time is the hard part. A video workbench for Claude Code and Codex. You say what you want in one sentence. The agent finds the idea, writes the film as code, checks its own work, and stops for your call at the concept and the first draft; when the film is long, heavy to render or costs money, it shows you the storyboard first too. **English** · [中文](README.zh-CN.md) · [Website](https://zlhad.top/OpenVideoHarness/docs/site/) · [Wiki](https://github.com/ZLHad/OpenVideoHarness/wiki) ![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-black) ![Agents](https://img.shields.io/badge/agents-Claude%20Code%20%7C%20Codex-orange) ![Engines](https://img.shields.io/badge/engines-HyperFrames%20%7C%20canvas%20%2B%20Three.js%20%7C%20p5.brush%20%7C%20Manim%20%7C%20Blender-blue) Twelve moments from real films made with it. More below, some with sound.
```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ZLHad/OpenVideoHarness/main/install.sh | bash cd ~/OpenVideoHarness && claude # or: codex ``` --- ## Why this exists Coding agents can already write a video. Give one a sentence and what comes back can startle you: real motion, real type, real rhythm. There are hundreds of films like that out there now. Ask again, and the same model loses the pacing, makes everything glow and invents a number. That isn't a rendering problem. HyperFrames, Manim and Blender turn code into pictures. None of them decides what the film is about, whether a line of text stays up long enough to read, or whether the number on screen is true. **What's missing isn't tools. It's craft.** This repo is that craft, written down where an agent can use it: how to find an idea that isn't the first one everybody has, why the sound comes before the picture, how to check a film you can't watch. A few rules never bend, and everything else is a default that a good idea can overrule. It grew out of real films. Each time one went wrong, the lesson became a doc or a check, and the next film started from there. ## What makes it different

A stock chart that is also a mountain range.		 It has an idea before it has code.
Two or three concept cards come first, each with a frame and a hook. It says what every other film on your topic looks like, then goes somewhere else.

Said at the first stop: "glass, cosmos, a starry sky… dizzying".		 You direct. It does the work.
It stops for you at the concept and the first draft; when the film is long, heavy to render or costs money, at the storyboard too. Want to decide the hook, the voice or the cover as well? Name them. Want none of it? Say "just make it".

Time is the only input. This flash is counted in microseconds.		 Every frame is a function of time.
So any frame can be drawn alone, in any order, in parallel. A render that stops picks up where it stopped. A few seconds of a finished 4K film can be redrawn and put back without touching the rest.

The agent going through its own frames.		 It can't watch, so it measures everything it can.
An agent can't see video or hear sound. So it reads contact sheets against a 20-point checklist, measures the sound, and hands the draft to a reviewer with a fresh context, who scores it on 8 points. bin/vh check catches frozen frames, flashes, subtitles too short to read and wrong colour tags, and names a way out of each.

▶ Press play and turn the sound on: each harmonic sounds its own note.		 Sound comes first, and it's code too.
The narration or the music goes down first. Every word and beat gets a time, and the picture hangs on those times. The score is written as code, and sound effects land on the frame where things happen.

A generated plate, with code on top, both on record.		 Real material, on the record.
Archive footage, generated pictures, recorded sound: one ledger keeps where each file came from, its licence and what it cost. No budget, no paid call.

From a film of 33 minutes.		 Long films hold up.
Shots, captions and chapters hang on the narration's words, so adding a pause moves the picture with it. Edit lists join pages and footage, renders resume, and the upload copy fits the platform's limit. The longest so far runs 33 minutes in 4K.
**And not one AI look.** Left alone, AI video drifts toward one face: dark background, glow, glass cards. Here are 32 of its 33 styles, all rendering the same sentence: ## What it makes Moments from a dozen films the author made with it in about a month, about 100 minutes in all. Physics, chemistry, engineering, money, folklore, literature, essays: each in a world of its own. They're in Chinese, and silent here.
